title: Quantitative MRI of Endothelial Permeability and (Dys)function in Atherosclerosis
protocol: Feed ApoE-/- mice a high-fat diet containing 21% fat from lard and 0.15% (wt/wt) cholesterol for up to 12 weeks to induce atherosclerosis.
Load an insulin syringe with the right volume of gadofosveset trisodium to achieve a dose of 0.03 mmol/kg, keeping the injection volume between 50-150 μl.
Place the cage on a heating pad set to 37 °C to pre-heat and maintain body temperature during the experiment.
Induce anesthesia by placing the mouse in an induction box lined with absorbent tissues.
Adjust the flowmeter to deliver 3%-5% isoflurane at 1 L/min of O2 for about 3-5 min.
Confirm correct anesthesia depth by identifying a breathing rate less than 70 breaths per minute and loss of withdrawal reflex to toe pinch.
Transfer the animal to a holder and insert its nose into a nose cone.
Maintain anesthesia through the nose with 1%-2% isoflurane at 1 L/min of O2 delivered via an anesthesia airflow in the holder.
Apply vet ointment on the animal's eyes to prevent dryness while under anesthesia.
Place the animal either prone or on its side.
Clean the tail with an alcohol swab.
Locate one of the two tail veins.
Warm up the tail with a UV lamp if necessary to make the tail veins more visible.
Insert the 29 G insulin needle parallel to the vein with the bevel facing up.
Gently inject the volume of the prefilled syringe containing gadofosveset trisodium.
Ensure there is no bleeding at the injection site after withdrawing the needle.
Wait for 30 seconds for gadofosveset to circulate.
Transfer the mouse to the MRI bed.
Cover the MRI table with absorbent tissues.
Place the MRI single-loop receiver coil on the MRI bed.
Use a platform to raise the receiver coil and avoid direct contact between the receiver coil and the MRI table.
Secure the coil to the platform using surgical tape.
Place and secure the tubing connected to a circulating heating pump around the coil set it to 37 °C.
Place the anesthesia delivery tubing into the bore of the MRI scanner.
Tape the anesthesia delivery tubing so that the nose cone reaches the tip of the receiver coil where the animal's head will be placed.
Turn on the in-bore camera to monitor the animal from the console room.
Use the software interface to start a new study for the animal.
Transfer the anesthetized animal to the scanner room.
Place the mouse in the prone position on the receiver coil.
Ensure the mouse's snout fits into the nose cone to maintain anesthesia.
Turn the anesthesia airflow to 1%-1.5% isoflurane at 1 L/min of O2.
Place the mouse on the MRI coil with its heart and neck regions located at the center of the receiver coil.
Secure the mouse's nose into the nose cone.
Tape the mouse's abdomen and tail to the platform.
Apply ECG conductive gel on the mouse's paws before attaching the ECG pads.
Attach four electrodes on the anterior and rear paws, ensuring the palm of the toes is completely open.
Firmly attach the electrodes to the platform using tape.
Align the laser of the scanner's bed with the base (proximal end) of the heart.
Use the clavicle and anterior paw line as a landmark for alignment.
Position the animal in the magnet's isocenter using an automatic MR table.
Start a scout scan to run the standard calibrations for the MRI system.
Set the monitoring equipment to detect the R-wave of the ECG.
Adjust the thresholds for each mouse and within imaging sessions so that there is reliable triggering.
Acquire a 3D gradient echo scan (GRE) to get multiplanar pilot images.
Identify the heart on the scout images, particularly on the coronal view, by its flow artifacts.
Plan a 3D contrast-enhanced MR angiography (MRA) scan in a transverse plane extending from the base of the heart toward the neck and carotid arteries with an 8 mm field-of-view.
Use maximum intensity projection (MIP) images to visualize the aortic arch, brachiocephalic and carotid arteries.
Plan subsequent late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), T1 mapping, and cine scans based on MIP and transverse MRA images.
Repeat the acquisition by moving the slices either proximally or distally if the level of the imaging volume is not correct.
Use the MIP and transverse MRA images to plan a single slice 2D-Look-Locker (LL) acquisition perpendicular to the ascending aorta or carotid arteries.
Set the heart rate to 60 bpm when using a simulated ECG signal.
Set a blanking period to ensure that the inversion recovery pulse interval is 1000 ms when using the recorded ECG signal.
Use Look-Locker images to determine the optimal inversion time (TI) for blood signal nulling required for the LGE scan.
Acquire an LGE scan after 20-30 minutes of gadofosveset injection, immediately following the LL scan.

Plan a transverse 3D fast gradient echo LGE scan to cover the heart base, brachiocephalic artery, and part of the carotid arteries with an 8 mm field-of-view in the foot-head direction using the same geometry as for the MRA.
Set the heart rate to 60 bpm when using a simulated ECG signal.
Set a blanking period to ensure that successive inversion recovery pulses occur at every 1000 ms for the LGE scan when using the recorded ECG signal.
Insert the T1 obtained from the Look-Locker into the LGE sequence under Contrast > Inversion Delay.
Use a 3D fast gradient echo acquisition to acquire transverse T1 mapping images 45 min after injection of gadofosveset.
Plan the sequence in the same orientation and geometry as the LGE scan.
Set the heart rate to 120 bpm when using a simulated ECG.
Ensure that the inversion recovery pulse between the two imaging trains occurs at every 500 ms when using the recorded ECG trace.
Prepare a solution of diluted acetylcholine in saline.
Load a 29 G needle insulin syringe with the right volume of solution to achieve 16.6 mg/kg.
Place a transverse slice across the brachiocephalic artery between the aortic root and the subclavian bifurcation using MRA and MIP images.
Acquire temporally-resolved cine images of the brachiocephalic artery with a transverse 2D gradient echo (GRE) using retrospective ECG gating.
Adjust the number of maximum cardiac phases to match the heart rate of each animal.
Gently inject acetylcholine intraperitoneally while the mouse is anesthetized in the scanner.
Wait for 6-10 minutes for the heart rate to stabilize and repeat the acquisition.
Return the mouse to its cage on a heating pad after imaging for recovery.
Export acquired images in DICOM format.
Use open-platform image analysis software for MRI segmentation and data analysis.
Drag Dicom files into the database of an open-platform software to load all the images.
Use LGE images to visualize contrast uptake in the vessel wall and calculate the area of enhancement as a surrogate marker of endothelial cell leakage.
Select both the MRA and inversion recovery scans.
Press Enter to load these images side-by-side.
Click on the small icon next to the scan name and drag and drop the MRA images onto the LGE images.
Select the option Re-sample to re-slice the MRA images using the LGE images as a reference to account for differences in slice thickness.
Click on the small icon next to the scan name.
Drag and drop the LGE images onto the MRA images.
From the menu, choose Image Fusion to overlay the LGE and MRA images.
From the toolbar, click on 2D Viewer, and then choose 3D Position Panel.
Use the buttons to manually correct for in-plane shifts to account for potential small displacements because of animal respiration.
Use the Closed Polygon tool located in the toolbar to manually segment the visually enhanced segment of the vessel wall.
Use the co-registered MRA and LGE images to guide the segmentation.
Segment all the LGE images that encompass the brachiocephalic artery.
Click on the Plugins button in the toolbar and choose ROI Tools.
Export ROIs to export the segmented area (mm²) for each region of interest (ROI) in a spreadsheet.
Sum the area of each slice to calculate the total area of enhancement in the brachiocephalic artery in the spreadsheet.
Use the T1 maps generated on the MRI scanner computer to calculate the mean T1 value of the vessel wall reflecting gadofosveset uptake into the vessel wall.
Load MRA and T1 map images and follow a similar approach as described above (steps 5.3-5.9) to segment the vessel wall and extract the T1 values (ms).
Invert the T1 values and multiply by 1000 to calculate the relaxation time R1 = 1/T1 in seconds.
Calculate the mean R1 for all slices covering the brachiocephalic artery in each animal.
Load phase contrast angiography images and velocity maps to calculate changes in vessel area and blood flow velocity during the cardiac cycle.
Segment both the images acquired before and after injection of acetylcholine to calculate endothelial-dependent vasoreactivity.
Use the semi-automated Grow Region tool to segment the lumen area (mm²) of the brachiocephalic artery in angiography images.
Use the Closed Polygon tool to segment blood flow velocity encoded maps.
Calculate the blood flow velocity (cm/s).
Export the lumen area and blood flow velocity data into a spreadsheet.
Identify end-diastolic and end-systolic cardiac phases from the exported data.
Calculate the percentage change in end-diastolic lumen area pre- and post-injection of acetylcholine.
Calculate the percentage change in blood flow velocity pre- and post-injection of acetylcholine.
Tabulate corresponding data derived from LGE images, T1 maps, and acetylcholine test for each animal.
Import tabulated data into statistical software for analysis.
